title: Infinitely Many Primes ≡ -1 (mod 12) and (mod 24) — Dirichlet Specialization
description: Answers OQ-01 from infinitude-primes-4k3 for the moduli q ∈ {12, 24}: there are infinitely many primes p with p ≡ -1 (mod q), i.e. p ≡ 11 (mod 12) and p ≡ 23 (mod 24). Both are obtained by specializing the repository's machine-checked Dirichlet theorem DirichletsTheorem.dirichlet_modEq (which delegates to Mathlib's Nat.infinite_setOf_prime_and_modEq) at the relevant residue. Each result is provided in two forms: the elementary % q = a statement and the analytic-matching (p : ZMod q) = a statement, bridged by two ZMod ↔ mod lemmas. 4 theorems, 2 bridge lemmas, 0 axioms.

overview.historicalContext: Dirichlet's theorem (1837) states that every arithmetic progression {a, a+q, a+2q, ...} with gcd(a, q) = 1 contains infinitely many primes. Its general proof is analytic, resting on the non-vanishing of Dirichlet L-functions L(1, χ) for non-principal characters χ. For special residue classes, however, far more elementary Euclid-style arguments exist. The class p ≡ -1 (mod q) is the most accessible family: for q ∈ {3, 4, 6} a direct product construction (à la Euclid's N = 4·n! − 1 for q = 4) suffices, and these elementary cases are formalized in the sibling files of this slug. The moduli q = 12 and q = 24 sit at the boundary of the elementary method — their unit groups (Klein-4 for 12, (ℤ/2ℤ)³ for 24) make a clean single-construction Euclid argument awkward — so this file instead specializes the repository's machine-checked Dirichlet theorem, completing the slug's spectrum-coverage table for the p ≡ -1 (mod q) family.
overview.problemStatement: **Open Question (infinitude-primes-4k3-OQ-01)**: extend the infinitude-of-primes-in-residue-class results beyond the elementary moduli to the full p ≡ -1 (mod q) spectrum. **This file's contribution**: settle the moduli q = 12 and q = 24, i.e. prove that {p prime | p ≡ 11 (mod 12)} and {p prime | p ≡ 23 (mod 24)} are each infinite, in both the % q = a and (p : ZMod q) = a formulations.
overview.proofStrategy:
**Route B (Dirichlet specialization)**. The repository file DirichletsTheorem.lean exposes `dirichlet_modEq {a q : ℕ} (hq : q ≠ 0) (ha : Nat.Coprime a q) : Set.Infinite {p | Nat.Prime p ∧ p ≡ a [MOD q]}`, itself a thin wrapper over Mathlib's `Nat.infinite_setOf_prime_and_modEq`.

For q = 12: prove `Nat.Coprime 11 12` by `decide`, instantiate `dirichlet_modEq` at (11, 12), then `convert` the `p ≡ 11 [MOD 12]` set to the `p % 12 = 11` set (the two differ only by unfolding `Nat.ModEq`, handled by `ext` + `simp [Nat.ModEq]`). The q = 24 case is identical at (23, 24).

The two ZMod-cast theorems rewrite the set `{p | (p : ZMod q) = a}` to `{p | p % q = a}` using the bridge lemmas `zmod_q_eq_a_iff`, then discharge to the elementary theorem. Each bridge is `ZMod.natCast_eq_natCast_iff` followed by `unfold Nat.ModEq; omega`.
keyInsights: **-1 is the canonical 'easy' residue**: across all q, the class a ≡ -1 (mod q) is the one most amenable to elementary infinitude proofs, because -1 is the unique order-≤2 unit shared by every (ZMod q)ˣ. For q = 12 the unit group is Klein-4 {1, 5, 7, 11} and 11 ≡ -1 is its distinguished involution; for q = 24 the group is (ℤ/2ℤ)³ and 23 ≡ -1 is simultaneously -1 mod 8 and -1 mod 3 under the CRT splitting 24 = 8·3.

**Specialization, not re-proof**: the infinitude content is *not* re-derived here. It is imported wholesale from `dirichlet_modEq`, which delegates to Mathlib's full Dirichlet theorem. The file's own work is the boundary glue: coprimality (decide), the ModEq-vs-% set identity (convert/simp), and the ZMod cast bridges (omega).

**Two formulations on purpose**: the `% q = a` form is the elementary statement a number theorist writes; the `(p : ZMod q) = a` form is what character sums and L-function arguments consume. Providing both, joined by an explicit iff bridge, lets downstream work pick whichever is convenient without re-establishing the translation.

**Why a sub-file, not a parent edit**: DirichletsTheorem.lean already houses the q = 4 and q = 6 specializations; adding q = 12, 24 there would mix slug-specific deliverables into the parent gallery entry. Keeping them in a dedicated sub-file (mirroring the slug's Klein2 and Tower sub-files) preserves clean attribution.

**The elementary frontier**: q ∈ {3, 4, 6} admit genuinely elementary (no-L-function) proofs of the p ≡ -1 class, and q = 8 is conjectured to as well; q = 12 and q = 24 are where the single-construction Euclid trick becomes unwieldy, which is exactly why this file routes through Dirichlet rather than a bespoke construction.

mainTheorems.name: infinitely_many_primes_11_mod_12
mainTheorems.significance: The q = 12 case of OQ-01: infinitely many primes ≡ -1 (mod 12). Proved by specializing dirichlet_modEq at (a, q) = (11, 12) — coprimality 11 ⊥ 12 by decide — and converting the resulting p ≡ 11 [MOD 12] set to the p % 12 = 11 set. 11 is the unique order-2 element of the Klein-4 unit group (ZMod 12)ˣ = {1, 5, 7, 11}.
mainTheorems.description: Infinitely many primes ≡ 11 (mod 12), via Dirichlet specialization.

mainTheorems.name: infinitely_many_primes_23_mod_24
mainTheorems.significance: The q = 24 case of OQ-01: infinitely many primes ≡ -1 (mod 24). Same proof shape as the q = 12 case, instantiated at (23, 24). Under the CRT splitting 24 = 8·3, the residue 23 is the unique element that is simultaneously -1 (mod 8) and -1 (mod 3) in the unit group (ZMod 24)ˣ ≅ (ℤ/2ℤ)³.
mainTheorems.description: Infinitely many primes ≡ 23 (mod 24), via Dirichlet specialization.

mainTheorems.name: primes_11_mod_12_zmod_form
mainTheorems.significance: Restates the q = 12 result in ZMod-cast form, the formulation consumed by character-sum / L-function arguments. Proof rewrites the set via the bridge lemma zmod_12_eq_eleven_iff to the % 12 = 11 set, then applies infinitely_many_primes_11_mod_12.
mainTheorems.description: ZMod-cast form of the q = 12 result.

mainTheorems.name: primes_23_mod_24_zmod_form
mainTheorems.significance: ZMod-cast form of the q = 24 result, by the same bridge-and-reduce pattern using zmod_24_eq_twentythree_iff.
mainTheorems.description: ZMod-cast form of the q = 24 result.

mainTheorems.name: zmod_12_eq_eleven_iff
mainTheorems.significance: Bridge lemma connecting the ZMod equality and the elementary modular form for q = 12. Proof: rewrite 11 as a Nat-cast, apply ZMod.natCast_eq_natCast_iff to turn the goal into 11 ≡ p [MOD 12], unfold Nat.ModEq, finish by omega.

mainTheorems.name: zmod_24_eq_twentythree_iff
mainTheorems.significance: Bridge lemma for q = 24, identical in structure to the q = 12 bridge.

conclusion.summary: For q ∈ {12, 24} the p ≡ -1 (mod q) case of OQ-01 is settled: there are infinitely many primes ≡ 11 (mod 12) and infinitely many ≡ 23 (mod 24), each in both the elementary % q = a and the ZMod-cast (p : ZMod q) = a formulations, with 0 axioms and 0 sorries. The infinitude is inherited from the repository's machine-checked Dirichlet theorem; the file's own content is the coprimality, the ModEq-vs-% set identity, and the ZMod cast bridges.
conclusion.implications: Combined with this slug's elementary sibling files (q = 3, 4, 6), the result extends Lean coverage of the p ≡ -1 (mod q) family to the moduli where a clean single-construction Euclid argument is awkward. The two-formulation pattern (elementary form + ZMod-cast form joined by an explicit bridge lemma) is a reusable template for any future residue-class infinitude entry that needs to interface with both elementary and character-theoretic downstream work.
